extracted.intended_audience: Researchers and applicants seeking grants from the John Templeton Foundation (academics, research teams, program officers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and evaluating grant applications to the John Templeton Foundation, especially for projects at the intersection of religion, science, and society. Covers core review dimensions, topical priorities, interdisciplinary expectations, application process, and award categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual Rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholarly excellence, methodological soundness, engagement with scholarly literature, logical coherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators look for strong scholarship and rigorous methods, clear engagement with existing literature, and internally coherent argumentation and design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Novel ideas, fresh perspectives, unconventional questions, methodological innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals should present new questions or approaches and demonstrate methodological innovation or fresh theoretical perspectives that advance the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Influence on field of study, societal impact, practical applications, long-term significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both scholarly and broader societal effects: will the work shift academic debates, inform practice or policy, and have lasting significance beyond the project period?

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary Relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Engagement across disciplines; bridging humanities, sciences, theology; multidimensional perspectives; cross-disciplinary collaborations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference for projects that genuinely integrate multiple disciplines rather than superficially combining fields; collaborations should produce multidimensional insights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with the Foundation's Mission
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevance to 'Big Questions' and engagement with areas such as character virtues, science of religion, free markets, genetics of human nature, and mathematical, physical, and life sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals should map clearly onto Templeton’s mission and priority topics (see Big Questions). Demonstrate how the project contributes to the Foundation’s core themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance to Religion, Science, and Society
rubrics_metrics.description: Advance collective understanding of how religious and spiritual beliefs and practices affect human flourishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitive projects explicitly address ways religion/spirituality influence human well‑being, social outcomes, or civic life; show conceptual clarity about 'human flourishing' and measurable pathways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive Engagement with the Sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Research that engages substantively and critically with the sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects should not treat the sciences superficially; they must engage methods, findings, and debates within relevant scientific disciplines and show critical interaction between humanities/theology and empirical science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust Interdisciplinary Collaboration (Philosophy/Theology informing Sciences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Robust interdisciplinary collaborations in which philosophical or theological understanding informs the findings and methods of the sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor collaborations where conceptual/theoretical work (e.g., philosophy/theology) influences empirical design, interpretation, or methods in science disciplines, rather than being merely adjacent commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key Priorities for Competitive Proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate potential to: intervene constructively in tensions characterizing modern life; clarify conditions that support meaning making; help individuals and communities cultivate better ways of being; show how interpretive frameworks, existential commitments, and communities form people into more resilient, fulfilled, and socially or spiritually attuned human beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals should articulate concrete pathways to these priorities—e.g., interventions, empirical tests, or conceptual clarifications—and explain how outcomes will contribute to practice, policy, or public understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary Integration (Special Application Considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate sciences with philosophy, theology, or religious studies through robust interdisciplinary collaboration; produce findings relevant to pluralistic societies; address individuals who may or may not claim religious affiliations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects should be designed for pluralistic relevance (not assuming a single faith perspective), show genuine methodological and conceptual integration across disciplines, and explain how results apply across diverse populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with Templeton 'Big Questions' (Topical Priority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Project topics that align with Templeton Big Questions such as free will and agency, character virtues, cognitive science of religion, cosmology and origins, forgiveness/gratitude/hope, human flourishing, generosity and altruism, limits of science and philosophy, consciousness, genetics and human nature, religion and health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should explicitly connect their research questions to one or more listed Big Questions and explain the contribution to that topical area; the list serves as a topical filter for relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application Process Requirements and Review Stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Many programs use a two-stage process: Online Funding Inquiry first; selected applicants invited to submit full proposals; external peer review; Strategic Programs Committee review; Board of Trustees final approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should follow the two-stage timeline, craft a concise inquiry that makes the case for fit, be prepared for external peer review, and understand final institutional decision points. Adhere to submission requirements and deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Award Category and Scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the appropriate category: discovery awards (small, exploratory), project grants (mid-size, defined goals), strategic awards (large, programmatic), conference and travel grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match proposal scope, budget, and timelines to the intended award type; small exploratory projects should propose feasible, focused aims, while strategic awards require program-level planning and broader impact strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational Stance and Values
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis on 'constructive engagement' between science and religion; pluralistic funding across religious traditions and secular perspectives; long-term commitment to building the field; welcomes nontraditional research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals that demonstrate constructive, pluralistic engagement and reasonable openness to unconventional approaches are viewed favorably. Applicants should explain how their work contributes to sustained field‑building and avoids partisan or exclusivist framing.
